Joe, these headlines build curiosity around Cadian's construction and setup; the supplied facts do not support a promise of better sleep or more energy.

1. Curious about grounding at bedtime?
2. What is stainless steel doing in a cotton sheet?
3. Grounding beneath the fitted sheet you already use.
4. A grounded outlet is part of this bedding setup.
5. See how Cadian grounding sheets connect.

Image: A provisional bedding illustration shows the cotton-and-stainless-steel underlay beneath the fitted sheet and its connection to a properly grounded outlet.

Joe, the concept makes the six separate cable positions easy to see.

**Headline:** Six cables. Each with its own place.

**Supporting copy:** Six separate loops keep your desk cables organised.

**CTA:** Shop the organiser

**Visual:** An original, text-led layout with a close view of six cables, one in each loop, so the practical payoff is visible. Use a warm white background, charcoal type and one muted accent colour as provisional art direction. For 1:1, place the headline above the product; for 9:16, stack the headline, enlarged product detail and CTA with more space between them. Without a supplied product photo, the product drawing remains a provisional illustration pending an accurate reference.

The everyday desk scene is a creative choice. Six loops are a useful selling fact even though competitors share it; the copy makes no exclusivity claim. No images generated.

Joe, here are the ad and a follow-up that answers the return enquiry first.

:::writing{variant="standard" id="68417"}
Try the mattress for 30 nights.

Pay $300 upfront and decide how it feels in your own bed. If it isn't for you, request a refund within the 30-night period. Return collection costs $40.

Explore the 30-night trial.
:::

:::writing{variant="email" id="68418" subject="How returns work during the 30-night trial"}
Hi,

You asked how returns work. You pay $300 upfront and have 30 nights to try the mattress. If you decide to return it, request your refund within that period. Return collection costs $40.

Reply with any questions about these terms.
:::

Before use, confirm when the 30-night period starts, the return-request method, refund timing and whether the $40 collection charge is deducted from the refund or paid separately. These details were not supplied. Drafts only; nothing sent.

Joe, Ad B produced the stronger observed first-order result despite buying fewer, more expensive clicks.

| Metric | Ad A | Ad B |
|---|---:|---:|
| Cost per click | $0.50 | $1.25 |
| Click-to-new-customer rate | 0.50% | 3.125% |
| Cost per new customer | $100 | $40 |
| First-order contribution before ads | $600 | $1,500 |
| Contribution after ad spend | -$400 | $500 |

At $60 contribution per first order, break-even acquisition cost is $60. B is below it; A is above it. These are contribution figures, not revenue or lifetime profit. Refunds and repeat purchases could change the eventual economics.

Healthy hook rates show initial attention, not qualified buying interest. A could attract less suitable visitors or create expectations its body, offer or destination fails to meet. A page or checkout problem is another possibility, not an established diagnosis.

Next, verify tracking, new-customer classification and equal attribution windows; compare audience, placement and timing; then inspect ad promises and the path from landing-page views through checkout. Non-random delivery means this does not establish that B's creative caused the difference. Use the investigation to design a narrower randomised comparison.

Joe, compare the working ad with one challenger, changing only the headline. Keep the original asset saved and available throughout.

| Decision | Plan |
|---|---|
| Question | Does a different headline reduce the cost of acquiring a new customer? |
| Control C | The existing image ad, with its headline copied verbatim into the test record. |
| Challenger T | Same ad with: "Six cables. Each with its own place." If that is already the control wording, use "Give each cable its own loop." |
| Hypothesis | Making the organiser's practical use explicit will attract more qualified buyers. This is a hypothesis, not a predicted lift. |
| Constants | Freeze the product image, headline font and placement, supporting copy, CTA, offer, destination, audience eligibility, placements, schedule and optimisation settings. Confirm the existing body supports the challenger; changing the body would make this a package comparison. |
| Allocation | Use a genuine random 50:50 assignment of eligible people to two mutually exclusive groups with comparable spend opportunity. Verify the actual assignment method. Automatic platform allocation between two ads is not necessarily random. |
| Main result | Spend divided by attributed new customers in each group, using one documented attribution window. Report contribution after advertising too, once product costs are available. |
| Diagnostics | Record impressions, clicks, landing-page views, checkout starts, purchases, refunds and any tracking or fulfilment problems. |
| Exposure | Propose seven complete days for an initial pilot, followed by the agreed purchase-delay window. Budget ceiling, acceptable acquisition cost and baseline conversion volume are currently unknown. The owner must set the spend ceiling before any launch. Seven days alone cannot establish a winner. |
| Review rule | Before launch, agree the smallest improvement worth adopting. If baseline volume becomes available, calculate the required sample and analysis assumptions. Otherwise treat the capped run as a pilot for estimating volume. Review once at the scheduled endpoint; stop early only for the spend cap, broken tracking, checkout failure or a predefined unacceptable loss. Do not stop because one version briefly leads. |
| Owner and state | Draft plan for the person managing the ads. No spend authorised and nothing launched. |

If volume and randomisation support the planned analysis, estimate the headline's effect with uncertainty. With sparse purchases, report the observed costs and an inconclusive result, preserving the control. Clicks can diagnose interest but cannot establish which headline sells better. Results apply to this audience, offer and period; a small test does not establish performance at higher spend.

Joe, keep the existing brand name and add one of these product names or descriptors beneath it.

| Candidate | What it communicates | Trade-off |
|---|---|---|
| Four-Compartment Cotton Picnic Bag | States the material, use and four separate compartments immediately. Familiar words make it easy to say and suitable alongside other plainly described bags. | Long and generic, so it offers limited distinction or memorability on its own. |
| Picnic, Sorted | Suggests the satisfaction of unpacking an organised picnic, supported by the separate compartments. Short and easy to say; it can fit a range of picnic accessories. Pair it with "Cotton picnic bag with four separate compartments." | The name alone does not identify a bag or explain its construction. "Sorted" may be less familiar in some markets. |
| The Picnic Four | Gives the four-compartment feature a compact, memorable product name. It could fit a range named by compartment count. Keep the plain product descriptor beside it. | "Four" could be mistaken for four-person capacity, which has not been supplied. It also sounds like "for" when spoken. Test that ambiguity before choosing it. |

My clearest default is **Four-Compartment Cotton Picnic Bag**. None implies cooling, waterproofing or a patented feature.

Still to check: whether intended buyers understand and later recall each name, fit with the existing brand and product range, competing names and search results, relevant domain needs, trademark availability and meaning in target languages. Those checks have not been performed.
